problem: The comparison operators are missing from the text. It reads "ordering (, >) compares item by item" — only the > survives and the < has vanished. The example sentence is broken the same way: "For example, [1, 2]  is True and [1, 2]  is True" states nothing at all, and a student cannot tell which comparison is being asserted.
fix: Write: "ordering (<, >) compares item by item, left to right, and stops at the first difference. A shorter prefix is smaller. For example, [1, 2] < [1, 3] is True and [1, 2] < [1, 2, 0] is True."

problem: The sentence "The changing methods below edit the same list object and usually return None" is contradicted by the bullets that follow it, because those bullets also list index(x), count(x) and copy(). None of these three changes the list: index and count return an integer and copy returns a new list. A student will conclude that count() or copy() can be used as a mutating method and returns None.
fix: Split the sentence: "The changing methods below — append, extend, insert, remove, pop, clear, sort, reverse — edit the same list object and return None. The non-changing methods index(x), count(x) and copy() return a value and leave the list as it is."

problem: The chapter says remove(x) raises ValueError if x is absent but does not say what index(x) does when x is absent. Under try/except questions this is exactly the gap students fall into, since both raise ValueError and neither returns -1 (unlike str.find).
fix: Add: "index(x) raises ValueError if x is absent; it never returns -1."

problem: "Some syllabi call this a reference copy" suggests a copy is made, but in b = a no copy of any kind exists — there is one object and two names. The phrase invites the very mistake the section is warning against.
fix: Write: "Some syllabi say b holds a reference to the same object; no copy, not even a shallow one, is made by assignment."
